9.title: How we built our multi-agent research system
9.author: Jeremy Hadfield, Barry Zhang, Kenneth Lien, Florian Scholz, Jeremy Fox & Daniel Ford (Anthropic)
9.why: Supervisor/worker from §2.2 written up as a production post-mortem rather than a diagram — read the sections on delegation instructions and on token burn, which are §2.3's context loss at handoff and §2.5's cost explosion described by people who paid for both.

9.title: Don't Build Multi-Agents
9.author: Walden Yan (Cognition)
9.why: The strongest published argument against everything today teaches — that agents must share full traces, not summaries — so read it directly against §2.3 and you'll be able to answer the client architect who arrives having already read it.

9.title: Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?
9.author: Mert Cemri, Melissa Z. Pan, Shuyi Yang, Lakshya A. Agrawal, Bhavya Chopra, Rishabh Tiwari, Kurt Keutzer, Aditya Parameswaran, Dan Klein, Kannan Ramchandran, Matei Zaharia, Joseph E. Gonzalez & Ion Stoica
9.why: Skip the methodology and read the MAST taxonomy itself — 14 failure modes observed across 1,600+ real traces, grouped into design / inter-agent misalignment / verification, which is a far better checklist for responsibility diffusion than anything you'd write from first principles.

9.title: Handoffs — OpenAI Agents SDK
9.author: OpenAI
9.why: Shows §2.1's claim — a handoff is just a tool call — as working code, and the `input_type` and input-filter sections are a typed handoff object and an explicit decision about what context crosses the boundary.

9.title: Multi-agent (LangChain docs)
9.author: LangChain
9.why: Compares subagents, handoffs, router and skills across three scenarios with model-call and token counts attached to each — the cost arithmetic of §2.5 laid out as a table you can lift into a client conversation.

10.title: Effective context engineering for AI agents
10.author: Prithvi Rajasekaran, Ethan Dixon, Carly Ryan & Jeremy Hadfield (Anthropic Applied AI team)
10.why: The single best framing of §2.5's context budget as a finite resource you spend rather than a window you fill, and it names compaction, note-taking and sub-agent offload as the three strategies with the trade-off each one makes.

10.title: Context Rot: How Increasing Input Tokens Impacts LLM Performance
10.author: Kelly Hong, Anton Troynikov & Jeff Huber (Chroma)
10.why: Eighteen models measured across growing inputs, including a needle-in-a-haystack variant with distractors — this is the empirical successor to Day 4's lost-in-the-middle paper and it is what makes 'more context is not free' a number rather than a slogan.

10.title: MemGPT: Towards LLMs as Operating Systems
10.author: Charles Packer, Sarah Wooders, Kevin Lin, Vivian Fang, Shishir G. Patil, Ion Stoica & Joseph E. Gonzalez
10.why: Read §3 (the memory hierarchy and the paging interface) and skip the evaluations — it is your virtual-memory intuition applied directly to the context window, which is the fastest route from 23 years of systems experience to the working/episodic/semantic split.

10.title: Memory tool
10.author: Anthropic
10.why: A memory store as a concrete file-backed API (view / create / str_replace / insert / delete) — useful because it forces the question §2.2 raises: which of the four memory types are you actually writing into it, and with what dedupe policy.

10.title: Context editing
10.author: Anthropic
10.why: Compaction as a shipped product surface — tool-result clearing, thinking-block clearing and summary-based compaction, each with a different thing it throws away, which is exactly §2.4's 'what each strategy loses' made checkable against a real implementation.

11.title: Architecture overview (Model Context Protocol)
11.author: Model Context Protocol maintainers / Anthropic
11.why: The primary source for §2.2 and §2.3 in one page — host/client/server with the 1:1 client-per-server rule stated outright, JSON-RPC 2.0 on the wire, and stdio vs streamable HTTP characterised the way you'd characterise any transport.

11.title: Understanding MCP servers (server concepts)
11.author: Model Context Protocol maintainers / Anthropic
11.why: Carries the table that makes the three primitives make sense — tools are model-controlled, resources application-controlled, prompts user-controlled — which is the distinction §2.4 hangs everything on and the one most MCP explainers get wrong.

11.title: Introducing the Model Context Protocol
11.author: Anthropic
11.why: The original announcement, and worth ten minutes purely for the framing you'll reuse in client meetings: the N×M problem of §2.1 stated by the people who chose to solve it with a protocol rather than an SDK.

11.title: Build an MCP server (quickstart tutorial)
11.author: Model Context Protocol maintainers / Anthropic
11.why: An hour with a real stdio server and a real host beats any amount of reading about the protocol — you'll hit the lifecycle, the tool schema and the 'never log to stdout on stdio' rule yourself, which is how those stop being trivia.

11.title: Equipping agents for the real world with Agent Skills
11.author: Barry Zhang, Keith Lazuka & Mahesh Murag (Anthropic)
11.why: Skills as portable procedural capability — a folder of instructions and scripts loaded by progressive disclosure — which is §2.8's contrast with MCP: MCP moves connections, skills move know-how, and the two solve different halves of the same problem.

12.title: Building A Generative AI Platform
12.author: Chip Huyen
12.why: The closest thing in print to the architecture review you're being asked to produce — context enhancement, guardrails, router/gateway, three cache layers, observability and orchestration, built up one layer at a time with the failure each layer answers.

12.title: The Tail at Scale
12.author: Jeffrey Dean & Luiz André Barroso
12.why: You almost certainly know this one, and today is when to re-read it with agents in mind: an LLM pipeline is a fan-out of slow, variable-latency components, so the tail-amplification argument applies directly to §2.3's p50-vs-p95 split.

12.title: How NOT to Measure Latency
12.author: Gil Tene (QCon San Francisco)
12.why: The definitive demolition of averaging percentiles and of measuring only what your load generator managed to send — watch it before you put a single latency number in front of a client, because the coordinated-omission trap is easy to fall into with agent traces.

12.title: Token & Cost Tracking
12.author: Langfuse
12.why: Shows what per-node cost attribution actually requires — usage captured per generation, prices resolved per model version, costs rolled up the trace — which is the plumbing behind §2.4's per-node cost table.

13.title: Using LLM-as-a-Judge For Evaluation: A Complete Guide
13.author: Hamel Husain
13.why: The 'critique shadowing' loop is judge calibration done properly — a domain expert grades a sample, you measure agreement, you fix the prompt, you re-measure — and the insistence on binary pass/fail with a written critique is the single change that most improves a judge you already have.

13.title: Who Validates the Validators? Aligning LLM-Assisted Evaluation of LLM Outputs with Human Preferences
13.author: Shreya Shankar, J.D. Zamfirescu-Pereira, Björn Hartmann, Aditya G. Parameswaran & Ian Arawjo
13.why: Read the sections on criteria drift and on the EvalGen interface — the finding that people only discover their real grading criteria by grading outputs is why §2.6's calibration set has to be built before the rubric is frozen, not after.

13.title: Interrater reliability: the kappa statistic
13.author: Mary L. McHugh
13.why: Six free pages that tell you what Cohen's kappa is actually correcting for, how to compute it, and — the part that matters in a client review — why the conventional 'substantial agreement above 0.6' bands are looser than they should be for anything consequential.

13.title: Testset Generation (Ragas)
13.author: Ragas maintainers (Exploding Gradients)
13.why: A working implementation of §2.2–2.3's generators, including the knowledge-graph approach to sampling chunk pairs — read it as a concrete alternative to the similarity-band heuristic, and note where it does and doesn't guard against unanswerable multi-hop cases.

13.title: Task-Specific LLM Evals that Do & Don't Work
13.author: Eugene Yan
13.why: A survey of which metrics survive contact with a real task and which quietly don't, with a strong section on classification metrics — the reason it belongs today is that regression gates need a metric whose noise floor you can measure, and most of the popular ones fail that test.

14.title: Practical BM25 — Part 2: The BM25 Algorithm and its Variables
14.author: Shane Connelly (Elastic)
14.why: Walks §2.2's formula one variable at a time against a toy index you can picture — set k1 to 0 and watch term frequency stop mattering, change b and watch length normalisation move — which fixes the saturation and IDF intuitions in half an hour.

14.title: The Probabilistic Relevance Framework: BM25 and Beyond
14.author: Stephen Robertson & Hugo Zaragoza
14.why: The primary source, by BM25's own authors — read §3 (the derivation of the term-frequency and document-length components) and stop there; the rest is a research monograph and you don't need it to defend the scoring function in a design review.

14.title: Retrieve & Re-Rank
14.author: Nils Reimers et al. (Sentence Transformers)
14.why: The clearest short statement of §2.5's bi-encoder / cross-encoder split — one encodes query and document independently so you can pre-index, the other reads them together and can't — plus working code for the two-stage pipeline.

14.title: Passage Re-ranking with BERT
14.author: Rodrigo Nogueira & Kyunghyun Cho
14.why: Four pages, and the paper that established the retrieve-then-rerank pattern everyone now ships — worth reading for the size of the gain over BM25 alone, which is the number that justifies the reranker's latency budget in §2.5.

14.title: The Use of MMR, Diversity-Based Reranking for Reordering Documents and Producing Summaries
14.author: Jaime Carbonell & Jade Goldstein
14.why: The 1998 original of the near-duplicate fix in §2.7 — a single λ trading relevance against novelty — and it is the same crowding-out mechanism as Day 10's semantic-memory decay, so reading it once buys you both.

15.title: Prompt caching
15.author: Anthropic
15.why: Read the cache-breakpoint placement rules and the write/read pricing table together — provider prompt caching is the one cache layer of §2.5–2.6 with no analogue in your existing intuition, and its rules (prefix-only, TTL, what invalidates a cache) decide how you order a system prompt.

15.title: Using server-sent events
15.author: MDN Web Docs contributors (Mozilla)
15.why: The SSE wire format, EventSource, custom event types and automatic reconnection with Last-Event-ID — everything §2.2's transcript assumes, including why a comment line works as a heartbeat against proxy idle timeouts.

15.title: GPTCache: An Open-Source Semantic Cache for LLM Applications Enabling Faster Answers and Cost Savings
15.author: Fu Bang
15.why: Short workshop paper laying out the semantic-cache architecture — embedding, vector store, similarity threshold, eviction — and it is the cleanest place to see why the threshold is a correctness knob, not a performance knob, which is §2.6's whole warning.

15.title: Fixing retries with token buckets and circuit breakers
15.author: Marc Brooker
15.why: Simulated comparison of no-retry, fixed-N retry, adaptive token bucket and circuit breaker — the reasoning transfers unchanged to a provider that returns 429s and 529s, and it tells you which of §2.4's layered-timeout-plus-retry designs actually degrades gracefully under a capacity event.

15.title: Guardrails — OpenAI Agents SDK
15.author: OpenAI
15.why: Input and output guardrails as tripwires that run in parallel with the main call — a concrete shape for §2.9, and the parallel-vs-blocking choice is precisely where the false-positive rate stops being a quality question and becomes a latency one.

16.title: Inside the LLM Call: GenAI Observability with OpenTelemetry
16.author: James Newton-King (OpenTelemetry blog)
16.why: Exactly §2.1's argument, worked end to end: a normal HTTP trace can't tell you what the machinery decided, and the GenAI semantic conventions add the attributes that can — with a real exported trace showing where the time and tokens went.

16.title: Traces
16.author: OpenTelemetry authors
16.why: The vocabulary §2.2's span table assumes — span context, attributes, events, links, status, span kind — and the section on context propagation is the part you need to get trace_id threaded through async tasks and the agent's step loop.

16.title: Sampling
16.author: OpenTelemetry authors
16.why: Head vs tail sampling stated plainly, including what tail sampling costs you operationally — read it right after §2.3, because '100% for errors and low ratings, 10% otherwise' is a tail-sampling policy and you should know what it takes to implement one.

16.title: Dapper, a Large-Scale Distributed Systems Tracing Infrastructure
16.author: Benjamin H. Sigelman, Luiz André Barroso, Mike Burrows, Pat Stephenson, Manoj Plakal, Donald Beaver, Saul Jaspan & Chandan Shanbhag
16.why: The origin of everything in §2.2, and worth reading today specifically for §4.4 on sampling — Dapper's uniform 1-in-1000 is the instrument §2.3 says is wrong for LLM traces, and seeing why they chose it makes the contrast sharp.

16.title: Observability: A Manifesto
16.author: Charity Majors (Honeycomb)
16.why: Fifteen minutes on the distinction that decides your whole design — pre-aggregated metrics answer questions you already knew to ask, high-cardinality events let you ask new ones — which is why §2.4 stores the full prompt instead of a hash.
